newsitem.title: GERMANY: Cash help mounts for German flood victims.
newsitem.headline: Cash help mounts for German flood victims.

text.p: Help is trickling in from at home and abroad for thousands of East Germans, swept from their homes by catastrophic floods, to rebuild their lives.

Three weeks into the flooding, the worst seen in eastern Germany in 200 years, mass circulation Bild newspaper on Wednesday placed an emotional appeal for citizens around Germany to send money to aid the flood victims.

"We will help -- an evening for the flood victims," Bild wrote in bold white letters set against a black background on the front page of Wednesday's edition, advertising an evening of live entertainment and reports about the flood on Sunday.
The newspaper encouraged readers to make donations to a bank account set up to rebuild the ravaged region.

Thousands of soldiers, aid workers and villagers have worked round the clock to prop up sodden flood barriers in an effort to stem the flooding, which has killed 100 people in neighbouring Poland and the Czech Republic.

The European Union proposed contributing 1.5 million Ecus ($1.6 million) in relief aid for the eastern state of Brandenburg -- a fraction of the one billion marks ($544.1 million) it estimates it will need to repair the damage.
The German federal government and the state of Brandenburg had already agreed to free up 40 million marks for aid.

In the private sector, Germany's largest bank Deutsche Bank AG, riding high on strong first half results, said it had donated half a million marks, while savings banks in eastern Germany had pulled together 1.5 million.
Calls for solidarity have reverberated throughout Germany, prompting compassion from all parts of society.
"We saw the pictures on television and wanted to help quickly and without much bureaucracy," football legend Franz Beckenbauer said after his club Bayern Munich donated 100,000 marks to the victims.
The works council of carmaker Volkswagen AG appealed to all workers to make contributions.
Aid organisations like the Red Cross are trucking food into the flood area and taking donations of any kind. "Our phones are simply ringing off the hook," a spokesman said in Berlin.

In a bid to help farmers, who have been hardest hit by the catastrophe, Germany's state-owned agriculture bank said it would offer loans at very favourable rates and cut out much of the bureaucratic paperwork involved in obtaining them.

Insurer Allianz AG promised to deal with claims quickly and efficiently. The group said it had set up a 24-hour hotline to field questions, and allowed its agents to authorise damages of up to 3,000 marks without checking back with headquarters.
In total, Allianz expects to make damage payments of at least 100 million marks, the group said in a statement.

To rebuild the flooded homes and farms, Federal Labour Office President Bernhard Jagoda announced more job-creation measures, helping both the unemployed and the victims of the flood, which may often be one and the same.
"Whatever we need will be created," Jagoda said, promising masses of new jobs. ($ = 1.837 German Marks)
